title: The Federal Remnant: What's Left of the United States Government
body:
# The Federal Remnant: What's Left of the United States Government

## The Denver Administration

The entity that still calls itself the United States Government operates from a fortified administrative complex in Denver, Colorado. It moved there in 2147 after Washington D.C. was rendered uninhabitable by a tactical nuclear detonation during the Corporate Sovereignty Crisis — an event whose perpetrators have never been conclusively identified, though the list of suspects includes three corponations, two foreign governments, and the federal government itself. The crater is still radioactive. The monuments are shadows burned into glass.

Denver was chosen for its geographic centrality, its distance from both coasts, and its altitude — a practical consideration in a world where sea-level cities have a lifespan measured in decades. The Denver Complex houses approximately 4,000 federal employees: a skeleton crew of administrators, a small diplomatic corps, a ceremonial military honor guard, and a legal department whose primary function is drafting memoranda that no one reads.

## Power Without Power

The Federal Remnant has the legal authority to govern 300 million citizens. It has the practical ability to govern approximately none of them. The corponations hold sovereign authority over their territories through corporate charters that predate the D.C. destruction. The military — what remains of it — was privatized piecemeal between 2140 and 2160, with individual branches absorbed into corporate security divisions. The nuclear arsenal was decommissioned after D.C., partly out of genuine horror and partly because the corponations did not want anyone else to have the same option.

What the Federal Remnant does have is legitimacy — or at least the ghost of it. International bodies still recognize the United States as a sovereign nation. Trade agreements still bear a federal signature. The UN General Assembly still seats an American ambassador. This ghost of legitimacy is worth money, and the corponations pay for it in the form of a negotiated stipend they call 'federal revenue sharing' and everyone else calls a bribe.

The stipend is approximately Φ2.1 trillion annually — collected by the corponations from their tier-based taxation systems and forwarded to Denver quarterly. It is enough to maintain the Denver Complex, fund the ceremonial military, and allow the President (a position that is technically still elected every four years by a voting population of roughly 12,000 registered federal citizens) to issue executive orders that the corponations acknowledge receipt of and then ignore.

## The Coasts

California is abandoned. The combination of the Cascadia Seismic Event (2138), the Central Valley Desertification (2145-2160), and the Los Angeles Firestorm Complex (2152) rendered the state functionally uninhabitable. Scattered settlements exist in the northern reaches — survivalist communities, off-grid enclaves, and what the Federal Remnant optimistically calls 'pioneer zones' — but the great cities of the California coast are ruins. San Francisco is half-submerged. Los Angeles is ash. San Diego was absorbed by the Tijuana Sprawl, which operates under Mexican federal authority.

The East Coast fared marginally better geographically but worse politically. The D.C. destruction triggered a cascading evacuation of the eastern seaboard's power structure. New York, already struggling with chronic flooding and infrastructure collapse, lost its financial sector to the GLMZ's quantum currency exchanges. Boston contracted to a fraction of its former size. The eastern seaboard cities are not dead — they are diminished, depopulated, and largely ignored by the corponations whose economic gravity has shifted decisively to the Great Lakes.

## What Denver Means to GLMZ

For most GLMZ residents, the Federal Remnant is an abstraction — a logo on old buildings, a name in history documents, a punchline in Circuit bars. Axiom's legal department references federal law when it is convenient and ignores it when it is not. The tier system, the corporate courts, the privatized infrastructure — none of these things are technically legal under the Constitution of the United States. All of them are functionally unchallenged.

But the Remnant matters to one group: the excluded. For the untier-ed population of the Gray Zone and the ungoverned zones, the idea of a government that exists for its citizens rather than its shareholders is not a punchline. It is a memory. Some of them vote in the federal elections. Some of them write letters to the Denver Complex. Some of them still believe.

The letters are archived. They are never answered.

## The Strategic Illusion

The corponations maintain the Federal Remnant for one reason that supersedes all others: the alternative is worse.

A United States that officially ceases to exist is a failed state. A failed state is an invitation. China, the European Federation, the Pan-African Union, the Russo-Siberian Compact — all of them have the military capacity to project force into North American territory, and all of them have economic reasons to want the Great Lakes freshwater reserves, the Iowa caloric output, or the orbital launch infrastructure. The only thing preventing serious annexation consideration is the legal fiction that the United States is a functioning sovereign nation with the theoretical capacity to invoke NATO Article 5 and the theoretical possession of a nuclear deterrent that was theoretically not entirely decommissioned.

The corponations understand this with perfect clarity. The Federal Remnant is not a government. It is a scarecrow — a flag on a pole that tells foreign powers 'this territory is claimed, and claiming it by force would be complicated.' The Φ2.1 trillion annual stipend is not a bribe. It is the cheapest defense budget in human history.

Every four years, the corponations ensure the presidential election is covered by international media. Every year, the Denver Complex issues a State of the Union address that foreign intelligence services analyze for policy signals that do not exist. Every quarter, the federal ambassador to the UN votes on resolutions that affect nothing. The performance is meticulous, and the audience is not the American public — it is every foreign government with a map and a navy.

The day the corponations stop funding Denver is the day the world stops pretending the United States exists. Nobody knows what happens after that. The corponations have modeled it. The models are classified. The budgets for the Denver stipend increase every year.
